name: Tri-Heal Max Protocol
lead: Tri-Heal Max Protocol is a name used by online peptide vendors for a three-peptide blend sold for tissue repair and recovery. People who use healing-peptide blends aim to recover faster from injuries and hard training so they can keep training consistently and keep building their physique.

The exact composition is set by each vendor and is not standardized, and the blend is sold for research use rather than as an approved medicine. Published human trials of the blend itself have not been located.

Healing-peptide blends of this kind may include BPC-157, a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide described by Predrag Sikirić in 1993 that has been studied mainly in laboratory animals; Wikipedia says athletes and the public use it mainly for injury recovery, that human evidence is very limited, and that it is not approved by any drug regulator for human use.[1]

chain: Multi-peptide blend taken for tissue repair
Aims at faster healing of tendons, joints and muscle
More consistent training and physique progress
angle.text: Users take healing-peptide blends to recover from injuries and hard training, which supports continued training and a better physique. The effect on recovery is what users report; it has not been tested in trials of this blend.

infobox: Sold as research chemicals; not approved as a drug

paras: The product is marketed as a combined protocol of three healing-oriented peptides. Vendors package it as one kit; names and ratios differ between sellers, so it is a brand-style label rather than a single defined compound.

BPC-157 was reported in 1993 in the Journal of Physiology, Paris. Pre-clinical studies suggest cytoprotective, neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects and faster tissue and organ healing. Human evidence is very limited and includes a retrospective study of 12 patients with knee pain and a pilot study in interstitial cystitis; a phase I trial in healthy volunteers did not have its results submitted.[1]
Because it promotes angiogenesis, Wikipedia notes it may promote cancer or enlarge cancers not yet detected, and health authorities discourage use because human safety data are insufficient.[1]
No studies found for this blend. Registered trials of unrelated wound-care products, such as amniotic membrane dressings for diabetic foot ulcers, do not test it.

Sellers label such products for research use only; they are not approved by regulators as medicines, and purity and contents are set by the vendor. Wikipedia reports BPC-157 has been banned by WADA since 2022, and that on 30 October 2026 the US HHS announced compounding pharmacies may supply it for human use despite lacking FDA approval.[1]

timeline.event: BPC-157 is described by Predrag Sikirić.[1]

card.summary: A vendor three-peptide blend that users take to speed recovery from injuries and training.
card.note: Unapproved research-chemical product; contents vary by vendor.

quick.overview:
Tri-Heal Max Protocol is a vendor-sold blend of three peptides marketed for healing and recovery. People use it hoping to bounce back faster from injuries and training.

Its composition depends on the seller.
quick.mechanism: Vendors describe the component peptides as supporting tissue repair. No published studies test the blend itself.
quick.risks: It is sold as a research chemical and is not an approved medicine. Product purity and contents are not regulator-verified.
